# Abstract

Fishery-independent indices of abundance are important inputs for stock assessments and empirical control rules to inform fisheries management.
However, changes in survey protocols may hinder the calculation of such indices if population abundance is conflated with changes in catchability.
Typically, when a survey vessel or sampling gear is replaced, comparative fishing (CF) experiments are used to estimate the relative catchability between vessels or gear configurations to calibrate expected catch rates.
However, when direct estimates are not available, we propose the use of spatiotemporal models to indirectly estimate the calibration factor as part of index standardization.
Indirect estimates are possible without CF data if the population process is not modeled independently across time steps.
Across six case studies for species with CF data, we show that indices from indirect calibration are similar in trend as those from direct calibration across the vessel change.
While the precision of the calibration factor is lower with indirect calibration than with direct calibration, indirect calibration frequently performed better than no calibration and provided a statistically rigorous approach to develop an integrated synthetic index.
We show how statistical diagnostics can support or reject the suitability of indirect calibration when comparison to direct calibration is not possible in real world cases.
Simulation experiments additionally supported the use of indirect calibration. 
While direct calibration remains the recommended approach, we propose indirect calibration as a potential tool when comparative fishing experiments are not possible.

# Introduction

Indices of abundance estimated from catch rates in research surveys are valuable for assessing and informing management of population trends in fish stocks [@maunder2003; @punt2010; @bentley2005].
Research surveys have protocols for sampling design with standardized fishing vessel, gear, and set locations to ensure catch rates are proportional to stock density and factors that alter catchability of the resource are minimized [@gunderson1993].
Changes in survey design are occasionally needed as vessels and fishing gear are replaced due to wear and tear, and new fishing gear employed in the survey may have a different catchability.
For example, changes in survey objectives can reduce the mesh size to maximize catchability of various species for stock assessment, or updates in technology warrant a new trawl design.

The ability to use catch rates across the change in survey methodology is compromised when catchability changes.
If the difference in catchability is not known, then there is effectively a break in the index of abundance time series, creating a discontinuity in a continuous monitoring program.
The discontinuity poses challenges for fisheries managers who rely on consistent long-term data to detect population trends, set catch limits, and evaluate the effectiveness of management measures. 
The old index becomes a historical series, but is less useful to inform trends relative to the current time period.
Considerable time is required to build the time series of the new survey, creating a period of uncertainty when the new survey is not fully utilized.

To mitigate these shortcomings, the relative catchability between surveys can be estimated through a comparative fishing (CF) experiment.
Before the retirement of the old vessel or gear, catch rates from the old vessel and gear are compared in a common set of spatial and temporal strata.
Assuming the underlying stock density is identical for both vessels and gears, the difference in catch rates in a joint set is attributed to relative catchability $\rho$, typically referred to as the "calibration factor" or "vessel effect" [@pelletier1998; @cadigan2010]. 
To develop the index of abundance across both vessels, catch rates from the old survey are adjusted by the calibration factor to obtain the hypothetical values had the new survey protocol operated throughout the entire time series.

Logistical challenges may preclude the possibility for CF experiments.
For example, in the Arctic, the research vessel (RV) *Paamiut* with an Alfredo III trawl that executed trawl surveys in NAFO Subareas 0 and 1 was decommissioned ahead of schedule in 2017 as it was no longer seaworthy [@hedges2023].
The replacement vessel, the RV *Tarajoq* utilizing a Bacalao trawl only become operational in 2022.
Thus, comparative fishing experiments were not logistically possible to calibrate indices between these two vessels.
As a result, a gap in the survey exists between 2017 and 2022 [@hedges2023].

This survey gap compromises the ability to provide science advice for the NAFO Subarea 0+1 (Offshore) Greenland halibut (*Reinhardtius hippoglossoides*) stock, where catch advice has historically been provided with an index-based control rule [@jorgensen2016]. 
The control rule adjusts the total allowable catch based on the trend in the index over the preceding seven years. 
Without calibration, managers need to wait seven years until data from the new RV *Tarajoq* survey to implement the control rule.
However, the control rule could be updated earlier if the index could be "stitched" with the old survey data.

This paper evaluates the potential to use spatiotemporal models to stitch indices in the absence of CF.
A spatiotemporal model is a form of a GLMM (generalized linear mixed model) used to predict patterns in stock abundance across space and time [@thorson2019], and is an increasingly popular and flexible approach to standardizing catch rate data from multiple sources to produce indices of abundance [e.g., @gruss2019; @webster2020; @monnahan2021].
This approach can impute abundance in unsampled time-area strata resulting from changes in survey sampling design [@yalcin2023; @anderson2025] or missing sets, otherwise not possible with a design-based index approach.
As with any other index standardization procedure, fixed effects and random effects can account for habitat or catchability covariates that affect catch rates [@thorson2014; @thorson2019].
We propose that $\rho$ be estimated as a fixed effect and then applied for all years of the survey to generate the population index.

An initial application demonstrated the approach for Subarea 0/1 (Offshore) population of Greenland halibut [@huynh2023]. 
An index was standardized from the survey from the RV *Paamiut* and the 2019 survey on the Fishing Vessel (FV) *Helga Maria*, accounting for differences in catchability between the two vessels.
Results supported field observations that the trawl on the FV *Helga Maria* did not catch small fish as efficiently as on the RV *Paamuit* at deep depths [@nogueira2020], and the spatiotemporal model calculated the corresponding index accounting for this gear behaviour.

This paper describes a novel application of spatiotemporal models to demonstrate how index calibration may be viable for case studies where CF data do not exist, expanding the utility of historical data with current biological surveys.
We provide a validation study to compare indices of abundance stitched together with and without CF data.
We also propose diagnostic procedures to identify whether calibration without CF data is suitable when applied to real data.
Finally, we use simulation testing to demonstrate the viability of the approach.

# Methods

<!--

## Calibration factors from comparative fishing

A "direct" calibration factor $\rho_\textrm{CF}$, the catchability ratio between the new and the old vessel, can be estimated from a comparative fishing experiment consisting of joint sets $i$ where the two vessels are fishing simultaneously in the same location at the same time. Thus, environmental covariates are expect to be identical for both vessels.

The calibration factor is estimated with a binomial model of the form:

\begin{equation}
\textrm{logit}(p_i) = \log(\rho_\textrm{CF}) + \log(E_{i,\textrm{new}}/E_{i,\textrm{old}}) + \epsilon_i (\#eq:cf)
\end{equation}

where $p_i$ is the proportion of total catch in joint set $i$ caught with the new vessel, $E_i$ is the effort, e.g., swept area for a trawl survey or number of deployed hooks in a longline survey, and $\epsilon_i$ is a set level random effect. 
The calibration factor can be estimated in a binomial GLMM where the intercept is $\log(\rho_\textrm{CF})$ and the offset is the log ratio of fishing effort of the new and old vessels. 
Under equation \@ref(eq:cf), differences in catch rates are primarily attributed to differences in catchability.
See @cadigan2010 and @miller2013 for further description.

## Calibration factors in spatiotemporal models

Index standardization with spatiotemporal models involves fitting survey catch rates at the set level, followed by predictions of stock density across a fixed spatial domain. The estimation model is typically of the form:

\begin{equation}
\log(y_i) = O_i + \sum_jX_{i,j}\beta_j + \omega'_i + \varepsilon'_i (\#eq:st)
\end{equation}

where response variable $y_i$ is the survey catch of set $i$, $O$ is an offset term accounting for effort, $\beta$ is a vector of fixed effects of length $j$, $X$ is the design matrix, $\omega'_i$ is the spatial random effect at the spatial location of set $i$, $\varepsilon'_i$ is the spatiotemporal effect at the spatial location and time step of set $i$ generated from a random walk, and the natural logarithm is the link function between the response variable and linear predictors. The prime notation denotes an interpolated value, as explained in the next paragraphs.

The design matrix consists of abundance or catchability covariates, as well as an intercept term.
To standardize catches, an effort covariate $E_i$, typically swept area for a trawl survey or number of deployed hooks in a hook and line survey, is included as an offset term (separate from the design matrix) with the appropriate link transformation, i.e., $O_i = \log(E_i)$. 

Spatial random effects $\omega_s$ are estimated as a Gaussian Markov random field (GMRF) at pre-defined vertices on a finite-element mesh at points $s$.
This GMRF is structured to approximate a continuous Gaussian random field with Matérn covariance using the stochastic partial differential equation approach [@lindgren2011]. 
The Matérn covariance function is estimated with marginal standard deviation $\sigma$ and de-correlation parameter $\kappa$.
The range is a derived parameter, where $r = \sqrt 8/\kappa$, that denotes the distance at which GMRF values are effectively uncorrelated in Euclidean units, and may be a more intuitive value to interpret spatial connectivity.

Similarly, spatiotemporal random effects $\varepsilon_{s,t}$ are estimated at points $s$ and time step $t$ with a random walk, where $\varepsilon_{s,t} = \varepsilon_{s,t-1} + \delta_{s,t-1}$, with $\delta_{s,t-1}$ drawn from a GMRF.
Bilinear interpolation along the finite-element mesh is then used to obtain the corresponding values for the spatial location of set $i$ [@lindgren2011]. 

Maximum likelihood estimation is used to estimate the fixed effects $\beta$, random effects ($\omega_i$, $\delta_{s,t}$), and nuisance parameters ($\sigma$, $\kappa$). In this study, the negative binomial probability distribution function is used for the likelihood where the variance is a quadratic function of the mean (NB2) [@hilbe2011]. 
Model fitting was performed with the sdmTMB R package version 0.7.0 [@anderson2024].
Example R code for the various models is provided in the Supplementary Material.

### Direct calibration

If the survey has a direct calibration factor from comparative fishing, then the catch rates can be adjusted by $\rho_\textrm{CF}$ in the offset, with $O_i = \log(E_i/\rho_\textrm{CF})$ for fishing sets from the old vessel and $O_i = \log(E_i)$ otherwise.

### Indirect calibration

If direct calibration factors are not available, then we propose to estimate an "indirect" calibration factor $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ as a fixed effect.
To do so, the design matrix includes a covariate $j$ that identifies fishing sets to vessel, i.e., $X_{i,j} = 1$ for the new vessel and $X_{i,j} = 0$ otherwise.
Because we use the log link function, the fixed effect corresponds to $\beta_j = \log(\rho_\textrm{ST})$.
Unlike equation \@ref(eq:cf), differences in catch rates can be attributed to either $\rho$, other covariates in the design matrix, or the population abundance when fitting the spatiotemporal model.

## Index standardization

After fitting the model, the index $I_t$ can be created by generating predictions of catch across grid cells corresponding to the spatial domain of the survey or stock for each year of the survey, applying the inverse of the link function, and summing the predictions across grid cells $g$:

\begin{equation}
I_t = \sum_g A_g \times \exp\left(\sum_jX_{g,j}\beta_j + \omega'_g + \varepsilon'_{g,t}\right) (\#eq:index)
\end{equation}

where $A_g$ is the area of grid cell $g$, using the approach of @thorson2015.
No offset in used in equation \@ref(eq:index). Therefore, with direct calibration, the predicted density is conditional on the vessel effect, i.e., the catchability of the new vessel, applied in all years.
With indirect calibration, the design matrix is updated in the prediction where the covariate for the vessel effect $X_{g,j} = 1$, so that the catchability of the new vessel is used for all years.

The year-specific Wald confidence intervals of the index time series can be obtained from standard errors calculated with the generalized delta method in TMB [@kristensen2016]. 
We also apply a generic bias correction to account for non-linear transformation of random effects [@thorson2016].
The index confidence interval is calculated using the standard error of the indirect calibration factor estimate.
Thus, uncertainty in $\widehat{\log(\rho_\textrm{ST})}$, where ^ denotes an estimate, propagates into the confidence interval for years with the old vessel (in contrast, direct calibration factors are usually treated without error during the standardization).

## Identifiability with indirect calibration

This approach raises the question of how $\rho$ is estimable without CF.
A typical index standardization estimates year effects corresponding to stock abundance as independent fixed effects, in which case, the year effects are confounded with $\rho$ when the survey protocol changes.
However, $\rho$ is identifiable if a predictive model for the population process over time is used, as demonstrated if an index standardization model were a linear regression or generalized additive model with respect to time (Figure \@ref(fig:simple-example)). 
In this simple example, the predictive model is the regression slope and there are sufficient degrees of freedom to estimate a discontinuity in the regression arising from the vessel effect as a second intercept term.

This approach can be categorized in the statistical and social science literature as a "regression discontinuity design" experiment, where a treatment effect is estimated around a cutoff threshold and differences in the response variable immediately before and after the cutoff are explained by the treatment effect [@thislethwaite1960].
For index standardization, the treatment effect is the vessel effect and cutoff is the point in time with the vessel change.
As with any regression discontinuity, this approach assumes all confounding variables that affect the survey catch rates at the cutoff are accounted for [@lee2010].

With spatiotemporal modeling, the population process, i.e., spatial density through time, is predicted from a random walk across time steps in the spatiotemporal random field, where the expected state of the system in the current time step is the realized state in the previous time step. 
This model structure is analogous to the linear regression in the simple example.
Data from the old vessel provide information on the characteristics of the random walk process which maintains its state in the absence of new data.
Departures from the predicted random walk across the vessel change are then ascribed by the model to the vessel effect.

## Case studies

The validation exercise consisted of standardizing indices from surveys with gear changes and corresponding CF experiments, with a total of six case studies from two surveys. 
The Newfoundland and Labrador trawl survey (NL) used the vessel MV *Gadus Atlantica* operating with the Engel 145 otter trawl prior to 1995 and was replaced by the CCGS *Teleost* with the Campelen 1800 shrimp trawl. 
Paired vessel tows in 1995 were used to estimate the gear efficiency between the Campelen and Engel [@warren1996].
Further description of the survey and CF data is available in @cadigan2023 and @warren1996.
Two species were used from this survey: Atlantic cod (*Gadus morhua*) and Greenland halibut in NAFO Divisions 2J3KL. 

The Northeast Fisheries Science Center Spring survey (NE) samples groundfish stocks in New England and U.S. mid-Atlantic coastal waters. During 1968-2008, the RV *Albatross IV* with a Yankee 36 trawl executed the survey. 
In 2009, the RV *Albatross IV* was replaced by the RV *Henry B. Bigelow* with a 4-seam, 3-bridle bottom trawl [@politis2014].
A total of 636 paired comparative tows were performed in 2008 to estimate calibration factors [@miller2010; @miller2013].
Four species were used from the NEFSC spring survey with differing spatial footprints: Butterfish (*Peprilus triacanthus*) in New England and U.S. mid-Atlantic, Redfish (*Sebastes fasciatus*) in the Gulf of Maine, White hake (*Urophycis tenuis*) in the Gulf of Maine and Georges Bank, and Yellowtail flounder (*Limanda ferruginea*) in the Gulf of Maine and Georges Bank.

These case studies span a range of characteristics in stock trend over time (declining, increasing, and stable), spatial distribution and patchiness (from the range parameter estimated in the spatiotemporal model), and magnitude of the calibration factor (estimated from comparative fishing).

For each case study, three indices were developed:

1. Index with direct calibration. Calibration factors estimated from comparative fishing, $\rho_\textrm{CF}$, are used to adjust survey catches prior to fitting the spatiotemporal model, representing the ideal situation. For the Newfoundland survey, the direct calibration factors $\rho_\textrm{CF}$ were estimated from the binomial GLM of the form described in Equation \@ref(eq:cf).
For the NEFSC spring survey, $\rho_\textrm{CF}$ were obtained from @miller2010 which used a similar approach.

2. Index with indirect calibration. Calibration factors are estimated in the spatiotemporal model, $\rho_\textrm{ST}$, representing the proposed approach when comparative fishing is not available.
3. Index with no calibration. No calibration factors are considered in the index standardization, reflecting a naive approach.

Comparison of the direct and indirect indices illustrates the extent to which $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ agrees with $\rho_\textrm{CF}$, and provides a form of validation of the proposed indirect calibration method. 
Assuming the index from direct calibration is the most representative time series, comparison of the indirect and no calibration indices provides the marginal value of the indirect method.
If indirect calibration provides an improvement over no calibration, then discrepancies between the direct and indirect methods should be smaller than those between the direct method and no calibration.

## Diagnostic procedures

The proposed indirect calibration approach would be used when $\rho_\textrm{CF}$ is not available, i.e., when the indirectly calibrated and uncalibrated indices are possible.
This would normally be the case in applied practice.
Diagnostic tests are important to evaluate whether estimates of $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ are credible. 
We propose and present several diagnostic tests for the above case studies:

1. Are estimates of $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ significantly different from zero? If not, then the calibration is not needed if catchability is not statistically different between vessels. A similar approach is utilized with comparative fishing data to determine the need for calibration on a species by species level [@trueman2025].

2. Do estimates of $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ correctly fail to detect a significantly different vessel effect in the absence of a vessel change? The standardization method was applied in the case studies when the comparative fishing data indicated a significant vessel effect (true positive test). The method should also be applied to a subset of the data series from a single vessel with a dummy year change specified in the spatiotemporal model (true negative test). If the method is performing as intended, then estimates of $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ should not be significantly different from zero.

3. Do estimates of $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ change over time as the new survey time series is built? The indirect calibration factor can theoretically be estimated in the spatiotemporal model after the first year of the new survey is complete. Unlike the direct calibration factor, which is estimated once from a single data set, the indirect calibration factor is re-estimated each time an additional year of data is available from the new survey. Thus, there exists the possibility of a retrospective pattern in $\rho_\textrm{ST}$, where the calibration factor undesirably changes from successive updates of the index. A well-behaved model should have little retrospective behaviour in the $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ estimate when the model is re-fitted with additional years of data following the vessel change.

4. Are estimates of $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ dependent on the time gap between surveys? Surveys are ideally conducted annually but complications in logistics can frequently delay implementation of a new vessel for a longer period of time. The basis for estimating $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ is the change in the expected catch rates following the end of the data series for the old vessel. Thus, $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ estimates may significantly differ if the time gap increases. For both surveys in the case studies, there was no time gap for the vessel change. Sensitivity analyses that exclude data to delay the start of the new survey can evaluate the importance of the time gap.

The true-negative diagnostic was applied to each case study by repeatedly fitting the spatiotemporal model to the new survey data (1995--2020 for the NL survey and 2009--2024 for the NE survey) with a dummy vessel change over six consecutive years (2005--2010 for the NL survey and 2015-2020 for the NE survey). 
The retrospective analysis fitted all years of the old survey and 1--6 six years of the new survey, with terminal years ranging from 1995--2000 for the NL survey and 2009--2014 for the NE survey). 
The time gap analysis fitted the model to all years of the old survey and excluded years at the beginning of the new survey (ranging from 1995--1999 for the NL survey from 2009--2013 for the NE survey). 

## Simulation study

We used simulation testing to determine the behaviour of the proposed standardization approach across a range of scenarios.
Stock density was simulated in a 50 x 50 grid spatial grid for ten years from a constant GMRF representing $\omega_s$ in equation \@ref(eq:st) and year-specific GMRFs generated from a random walk representing $\varepsilon_{s,t}$ (Figure \@ref(fig:sim-grid)).
One hundred random sites were sampled in each year, where the cell density is predicted by equation \@ref(eq:st) and the simulated observations weres generated by sampling the negative binomial probability density function (pdf).

A total of 24 scenarios were developed from a factorial grid that varied four parameters of the operating model (Table \@ref(tab:sim-summary)):

1. Spatial density pattern: the operating model was generated with either a low or high de-correlation rate $\kappa =$ of 25 and 50, respectively, in the GMRF. A low de-correlation rate indicates that spatial stock density is highly correlated between adjacent cells (Figure \@ref(fig:sim-grid)). These $\kappa$ values correspond to range values of 0.11 and 0.06, respectively.

2. Magnitude of vessel effect: samples were simulated with a vessel change starting in year 6, with three levels of $\log(\rho) =$ 0, 0.2, or 1.
The scenarios with $\log(\rho) = 0$ provide an opportunity to evaluate performance in the absence of an underlying vessel effect.

3. Dispersion: samples were simulated with either high or low dispersion, with $\phi =$ 0.2 and 4, respectively, in the negative binomial pdf. The variance is a quadratic function of the mean $\mu$, with variance $\mu + \mu^2/\phi$.

4. Autocorrelation in spatiotemporal field: samples were simulated with either a lag-1 autocorrelation coefficient $\psi$ = 0.75 in the spatiotemporal field, where $\varepsilon_{s,t} = \psi\times\varepsilon_{s,t-1} + \delta_{s,t}$, or random walk to match the estimation model, i.e., $\psi$ = 1.

For each scenario, there was a single realization of the GMRF in the operating model (preliminary simulations with multiple realizations per scenario indicated similar results). The values of the marginal standard deviations were 3 and 1 for the spatial and spatiotemporal GMRF, respectively, using the average value estimated from the case studies in this paper.

There were one hundred simulation replicates ($n=100$) from sampling the probability density function. 
The GMRF was generated from the `sdmTMB_simulate()` function in the sdmTMB R package and the `rnegbin()` function from the MASS R package was used to generate simulated observations [@venables2002].
For each simulation, the spatiotemporal model was then fitted in sdmTMB, either estimating the indirect calibration factor or estimating no calibration factor.
For each fit, the corresponding index was generated.

Three performance metrics were calculated to evaluate performance:

1. The error in $\log(\rho)$, where the error is $\hat{X} - X$, the difference between the estimated value $\hat{X}$ and the true value $X$ of a model quantity.
2. The coverage in $\widehat{\log(\rho)}$, the frequency that the 95% confidence interval of the estimate included the true value of the parameter.
3. The root mean square error (RMSE) in the index trend, where $\textrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat{X_i} - X_i)^2}$, and $n$ is the number of simulation replicates. The index trend is defined as the slope in the regression of the log of the index over the most recent 5 years, and is intended to compare the estimated trend in the indices across the survey break.

Two additional diagnostics were performed within the simulation. 
First, a retrospective analysis was applied such that the model was re-fitted between 1--4 years of the new survey series.
Second, the models were re-fitted by excluding the start of the new survey to increase the time gap from 1 to 4 years between surveys, where the last data points of the survey are unchanged at 10 years.
For both, the performance metrics were calculated for fit for the retrospective and time gap analyses.

# Results

## Comparison of calibration factors

There was overlap in the confidence intervals (CIs) between the indirect and direct calibration factors in five out of six case studies (excluding NE Redfish, Figure \@ref(fig:rho2)). The extent of overlap varies: for NL Greenland halibut, there is some overlap in the CI, whereas for the remaining four case studies, the CI of the indirect factor subsumes the CI of the direct factor.

Generally, the indirect calibration factor is less precise than the direct calibration factor (Table \@ref(tab:rho), Figure \@ref(fig:rho2)).
However, this difference in precision is also attributable to differences in modeling assumptions, where the direct factor is estimated from comparative fishing sets where differences in catch rates is solely attributed to the vessel effect while the indirect factor is estimated from a more flexible model with multiple explanatory factors.
Nonetheless, comparison of indices with the two factors are consistent with common practice as direct factors are usually treated without error in index standardization.

## Comparison of indices

Two different behaviours were observed when comparing of indices of abundance with indirect and direct calibration factors.
First, the two types of indices frequently overlapped, with consideration the standard errors in the time series, in four out of six case studies (Figure \@ref(fig:index-compare)). 
For NL Cod, there was a strong agreement between $\rho_\textrm{CF}$ and $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ (with slightly larger confidence interval in the latter), which resulted in significant overlap in the indices for the old vessel.
The declining trend prior to the vessel change is clear with either calibration factor, and indirect calibration is preferred over no calibration.

For NE Butterfish, NE W. hake, and NE Y. flounder, the indirectly calibrated index was more uncertain for years with the old vessel, but the confidence intervals had substantial coverage and overlap with the directly calibrated index.
For NE Butterfish, the $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ estimate had the reverse sign from $\rho_\textrm{CF}$. 
Despite this result, the indirect calibrated index ultimately remained plausible because the trends in the index did not appreciably change with any calibration method through the break in the survey.
For NE W. hake and NE Y. flounder, the indirect calibration factors were slightly larger than the direct ones (Table \@ref(tab:rho)).
Nonetheless, the indirectly calibrated index is preferred over no calibration for these two species, because the index from indirect calibration overlaps with that from direct calibration than with no calibration.

Second, there was less overlap between the indirectly and directly calibrated index, with the larger indirect calibration factors, observed for the remaining two case studies (NL G. halibut and NE redfish).
For NL G. halibut, the indirect index infers that the stock did not increase as rapidly through the break in the index; some of the difference in catchability is assigned to the population process instead in the indirect calibration.
Nonetheless, the indirect calibration is preferred over no calibration.
For NE redfish, the indirect index infers that the stock increased and then plateaued earlier than in the direct index. For this case study, the indirect calibration overstates the vessel effect and is not preferred over no calibration. 
However, it is possible to distinguish this case study from the other five species through diagnostic procedures (next section).

## Diagnostic procedures

Table \@ref(tab:diagnostic-summary) provides a summary of the results of the diagnostics in the six case studies. The indirect calibration factor $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ was significantly different from zero in all but one case study, i.e. NE Butterfish (Tables \@ref(tab:rho) and \@ref(tab:diagnostic-summary)).
Notably, the direct calibration factor $\rho_\textrm{CF}$ for NE Butterfish was the smallest in our study, and indirect calibration did not substantially alter the index compared to the other two calibration choices (Figure \@ref(fig:index-compare)).

The true negative test correctly failed to detect a significant indirect calibration factor in the vast majority of cases (Figure \@ref(fig:rho-null)).
Although there was high variability among $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ estimates, depending on the dummy year change, false positives were detected in only 3/36 cases (approximately 8 percent), consistent with the predicted 5% false positive rate using the hypothesis test with significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ and 95% confidence intervals.

The retrospective analysis, conditional on zero time gap in the survey, indicated that indirect calibration factors were consistently estimated, and the magnitude of $\rho_\textrm{CF}$ did not systematically change with the length of the survey time series (Figure \@ref(fig:rho-ret)). 
The indirect calibration factors remained within range of the direct calibration factors for five of the six case studies, where there remained overlap in the confidence intervals between $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ and $\rho_\textrm{CF}$.

On the other hand, as the time gap between surveys increased, the indirect calibration factor was less consistently estimated (Figure \@ref(fig:rho-gap)). 
The point estimates were less stable, for example, with the calibration factor decreasing in the case of NL G. halibut and NE Y. flounder with increasing time gap. 
The standard error also tended to increase with increasing time gap, for example, almost as much as double when the time gap increased from 1 to 5 years for NE Y. flounder, and would create large confidence intervals in the resulting index.

The slope from a linear regression of the point values in Figures \@ref(fig:rho-ret) and \@ref(fig:rho-gap) was used to evaluate the presence of a trend in calibration factors in the retrospective analysis and the time gap between surveys. Ideally, the slope would not be significantly different from zero. 
For these two diagnostics, the slope was significant for NE Redfish (Table \@ref(tab:diagnostic-summary)), indicating inconsistency and instability in calibration factors through time for this species.

## Simulation testing

The error and coverage in the indirect calibration factor are shown in the Supplementary Material.
The $\rho_\textrm{ST}$ estimates showed some bias, where the median error was consistently above zero, across various model fits with the random walk operating models (Figure S1-S2). 
However, the random walk estimation model performed better against the AR1 operating models as the median error was close to zero and the range in error was smaller.
The error in $\rho$ was smaller with lower dispersion, i.e., $\phi = 0.2$, in the observation error and decreased as more data from the new vessel became available (Figure S1).
The most improvement in decreasing the range of error in $\rho$ was seen once the model was fitted with 2 years of the new survey (Figure S1).
On the other hand, the error increased as the time gap between surveys increased, particularly once the gap increased to 3--4 years (Figure S2). 
These trends in the error of $\rho$ did not substantially differ with various magnitudes of $\rho$. 

The coverage of $\rho$ was consistently high under the AR1 operating models (Figure S3-S4).
Under the random walk operating models, coverage was highest with high spatial correlation (low $\kappa$) and low dispersion for all three calibration factors. 
For other combinations of spatial correlation and dispersion, coverage was substantially lower with either an extensive time series of the new vessel (in the retrospective analysis, Figure S3) or the survey gap was small (Figure S4).
This behavior indicates the standard errors are sufficiently wide with fewer data, and is overly precise with more data.

With indirect calibration, the RMSE in the index trend was lower with low spatial correlation ($\kappa = 50$) than with high correlation, particularly in the random walk operating model (Figures \@ref(fig:sim-trend)--\@ref(fig:sim-trend2).
RMSE of the indirectly calibrated index also did not substantially change with $\rho$.
Importantly, RMSE was lower with indirect calibration than no calibration.
As expected, the difference in performance grew as the calibration factor was larger, indicating that indirect calibration was increasingly preferable.
RMSE decreased with more data and years from the new vessel, where the decline in error is most notable in the random walk operating models (Figure \@ref(fig:sim-trend)).

On the other hand, when the time gap between surveys increased, the index trend RMSE gap did not substantially increase (Figure \@ref(fig:sim-trend2)). 
The error in the $\rho$ estimate did not systematically affect the indirectly calibrated index across a wider survey gap.
While the error between the indirectly calibrated and uncalibrated indices was frequently similar, we found situations where the calibration method performed much better, i.e., with high $\rho$ and the AR1 operating model.

# Discussion

While empirical data from comparative fishing is desirable for survey calibration, the proposed indirect calibration may be a valuable tool and a practical alternative if the comparative fishing is not possible.
Comparison of the directly and indirectly calibrated indices of abundance indicates promising potential for the latter.
In the best case scenario, estimates of the vessel effect for NL Cod were similar despite estimation from different datasets.
In almost all cases (5/6), indirectly calibrated indices were also preferred over uncalibrated indices.
Overlap in the error bars of the directly and indirectly calibrated indices indicate a strong level of agreement in the interpretation of stock trends across the change in survey vessel, but often with increased uncertainty for the indirectly calibrated index.

The simulation study generally supported the key findings from the case studies. 
With a large vessel effect, indirect calibration was preferred over no calibration, while indirect calibration did not worsen index trends when there was a small or no vessel effect.

While the half of the simulation operating models match the estimation model (best-case scenario), the random walk structure in the estimation model allows the variance to grow over time.
Real population dynamics can have heavy-tailed distributions (with occasional large perturbations) or changing variance structure, either would affect the model predicted state at the survey vessel change and the uncertainty around it. 
The random walk is intended to prevent underestimation of process variance and misattributing population departures to the vessel effect.
The simulations also demonstrated that the estimation model performed better in the simple case where the population has a finite variance with AR1 operating model.

## Diagnostics

Statistical diagnostics are important analyses that can support use of the indirect calibration factor, especially if indices of abundance are used in a management setting.
Indirect calibration performed favorably with respect to the true negative test and the retrospective analysis.
The retrospective analysis suggested that the model estimates the survey calibration factor primarily from the first year of the new data. 

It is possible to estimate the calibration factor once and use the same estimate for all subsequent updates of the index.
While this approach would lose the error propagation properties demonstrated here, Bayesian approaches may incorporate priors on calibration factors, either indirect or direct, to incorporate calibration uncertainty in the index.
We generally support incorporating uncertainty of calibration factors in index standardization, following the recommendation by @cadigan2023, especially when these factors are not well estimated.

<!--
Direct calibration estimates were more precise than indirect estimates from the spatiotemporal model, as the former are frequently not estimated in spatially explicit models.
An alternative approaches to direct calibration could include fitting the index standardization model with the comparative sets, assuming the comparative sets are located in similar time and area strata, including seasonality, as the main survey.
-->

The time gap between surveys had the most notable impact on model results and is an important consideration if there is a long time gap between surveys.
Statistical diagnostics can indicate whether indices of abundance from indirect calibration are suitable.
Long time gaps may generate large standard errors, which could obscure trends in the index across the vessel change due to the uncertainty in the calibration factor.

The proposed diagnostics are logical tests that serve as necessary but not sufficient conditions for well-behaved models. 
As such, some judgement may be necessary to determine whether an estimated calibration factor is credible or not, for example, when the estimated catchability for a species may be lower with newer gear although the mesh size is smaller, or differences in catchability is quite extreme.
The diagnostics showed that indirect calibration did not work well for NE Redfish.
The model smoothens the index time series across the survey break in Figure \@ref(fig:index-compare), but to do so, the indirect calibration factor is much larger than the direct factor.

The retrospective analysis showed that the calibration factor was decreasing with more data from the new survey.
It is likely that the model conflates the vessel effect with abundance, i.e, new survey data impacts the calibration estimate although there should not be any information to do so.
Recent stock assessments for NE Redfish indicate strong pulses of recruitment in the 2000s [@nefsc2025].
Departures from modeled process variance in the form of strong cohorts would persist through time and continually challenge the calibration model as new data come in.

This behaviour contrasts with NL Cod, where the index is smoothened across the survey break but the diagnostics performed better, i.e., no retrospective trend in calibration factors.
In future case studies, trends in the calibration factor from successive fits is a likely indicator of poor performance, as inconsistency in estimates reduces reliability and confidence in the calibration.

More generally, if statistical diagnostics fail, analysts should try to understand the models or trends in the data that cause the failure, and simulations conditioned on the data at hand can be used to try to replicate the issue. 
Alternative model configurations are possible and may exhibit better performance. 
An autoregressive process or a smoother on the annual intercept terms are potentially viable alternatives, although the former assumes a finite variance structure and performance needs to be evaluated. 
Indirect calibration should be feasible when there is a unique expectation on the spatial density at the time step of the vessel change.
In contrast, the predicted spatial density with IID (independent, identically distributed) spatiotemporal fields is based on the long-term spatial pattern, and is not expected to perform well.

## Future applications

In real applications, some diagnostics are not immediately available.
Indirect calibration is possible with one year of new survey data, but a retrospective analysis of indirect calibration is not possible until additional years of the new survey become available.
Self-simulation techniques that use GMRFs conditioned on the historical survey data and test hypothetical vessel changes in the past can provide some insight on whether the system dynamics pose any potential problems for indirect calibration.
In any event, simulation results suggested that at least two years of data from the new survey are preferred to reduce error in the calibration.
Additionally, practitioners with a time gap in their surveys cannot reduce it, although the time gap can be extended further to evaluate if the calibration factor is stable or degrading.

We applied the spatiotemporal model and estimated vessel effects aggregated across all size classes. 
Frequently, catchability differences in fishing gears alters the size composition of fish caught and survey calibration factors are estimated as function of length [e.g., @fryer2003; @benoit2003; @lewy2004; @miller2013].
Indirect calibration by size class is possible by fitting separate spatiotemporal models for each size class or multivariate models [@huynh2023; @thorson2019comp; @perretti2019]. 
However, computation time and numerical stability will limit the feasibility of fitting models at a fine resolution, e.g., 1 cm bins, as is usually done with direct calibration [@miller2013]. 
It will be more computationally convenient to aggregate and use as few size categories as necessary to estimate size-specific calibration factors.
Nonetheless, the calibration methods presented here based on total catch by set are pertinent when insufficient sample sizes across size classes preclude length-specific calibration [@trueman2025].

Indirect calibration is not a panacea to avoid the calibration experiment given the value of fishery-independent surveys [@dennis2015]. 
We showed the higher uncertainty of the indirect calibration factor as the main cost of not having performed a calibration experiment. 
If there is high uncertainty in the estimate, then analysts can consider the utility of indirect calibration on a case by case basis.
Indirect calibration also requires an assumption that the population at the time of the vessel change is well behaved and can be modeled following trends in the data in prior years. 
Extreme events such as large mortality or recruitment events around the time of the vessel change will confound the indirect calibration factor, as was suspected for our NE Redfish case study.
Concomitant data sources independent of the survey, e.g., fishery CPUE or age composition to identify strong recruitment events, could support or reject indirect calibration if there is suspected confounding.

When direct calibration factors are available, we demonstrated the index standardization subsequent to the calibration analysis, but alternative approaches are possible. 
For example, comparative fishing sets can be included in the standardization model, where the direct calibration factor is also estimated in the spatiotemporal model.
In doing so, the calibration factor could be estimated as a spatially varying effect [@gruss2023; @trueman2025].
This approach may be desirable when gear behavior changes due to habitat differences by area, e.g., fishing at deeper depths or availability of different size classes of fish.

# Conclusions

We demonstrate that survey calibration remains viable when comparative fishing data are not available.
Such calibration can be implemented in standard open-source software, e.g., sdmTMB and VAST, which lowers the barrier to adoption.
Simulation work and diagnostics can provide validation of whether indirect calibration factors are credible.
From our study, we recommend at least two years of data from the new survey to perform indirect calibration, and a retrospective evaluation to ensure that calibration factors are not drifting as new survey data are used.

```{r sim-summary, results="asis"}
sim_summary <- readr::read_csv(here::here("tables/sim-summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

flextable(sim_summary) %>%
  set_caption("Parameters of the spatiotemporal operating model used in the simulation study.") %>%
  width(j = 1, width = 3)
```

```{r rho, results="asis"}
options(digits = 2)
case_study <- c("NL Cod", "NL G. halibut", "NE Butterfish", "NE Redfish", "NE W. hake", "NE Y. flounder")
case_study_label <- c("NL Cod*", "NL G. halibut*", "NE Butterfish*", "NE Redfish", "NE W. hake*", "NE Y. flounder*")

rho_CF <- readr::read_csv(here::here("tables/rho_CF.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(log_rho = format(log_rho),
         lower = format(lower),
         upper = format(upper),
         rho_CF = paste0(log_rho, " (", lower, " - ", upper, ")"),
         CF_SE = format(se, nsmall = 2))
rho_ST <- readr::read_csv(here::here("tables/rho_ST.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(Estimate = format(Estimate),
         lower = format(lower),
         upper = format(upper),
         rho_ST = paste0(Estimate, " (", lower, " - ", upper, ")"),
         ST_SE = format(`Std. Error`))

rho <- left_join(
  rho_CF %>% select(Name, rho_CF, CF_SE),
  rho_ST %>% select(Name, rho_ST, ST_SE),
  by = "Name"
) %>%
  mutate(Name = case_study_label[match(Name, case_study)] |> factor(case_study_label)) %>%
  arrange(Name) %>%
  rename(`Case study` = Name)

flextable(rho) %>%
  align(j = 2:5, align = "right", part = "all") %>%
  width(j = c(1, 2, 4), width = 1.5) %>%
  set_caption(
    caption = "Estimates of the survey calibration factor, log(\u03C1), from the comparative fishing (CF, \"direct\") and the spatiotemporal model (ST, excluding CF sets, \"indirect\") with standard errors (SE). The 95 percent confidence interval is provided in parentheses. Asterisks in the case study name indicate that confidence intervals of the two calibration factors overlap. Visual comparison of estimates are also shown in Figure 3. "
  ) %>%
  flextable::compose(j = c(3, 5), part = "header", value = as_paragraph("SE")) %>%
  flextable::compose(
    j = 2, part = "header", value = as_paragraph(as_chunk("log \u03C1"), as_sub("CF"))
  ) %>%
  flextable::compose(
    j = 4, part = "header", value = as_paragraph(as_chunk("log \u03C1"), as_sub("ST"))
  )
```

```{r ST-par, results="asis"}
options(digits = 2)
st_pars <- readr::read_csv(here::here("tables/ST_par.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  filter(!parameter %in% c("log(rho)", "Intercept")) %>%
  mutate(Name = factor(Name, case_study)) %>%
  mutate(Estimate = round(Estimate, 2)) %>%

  rename(Parameter = parameter)

flextable(st_pars) %>%
  align(j = 2:7, align = "right", part = "body") %>%
  set_caption(
    caption = as_paragraph("Estimates of the spatial random field standard deviation (\u03C3", as_sub("O"), "), spatiotemporal random field standard deviation (\u03C3", as_sub("E"), "), range (km), and negative binomial dispersion parameter (\u0278) in the indirect calibration model for the six case studies.")
  ) %>%
  flextable::compose(
    i = 1:4, j = 1,
    value = c(
      as_paragraph("\u03C3", as_sub("O")),
      as_paragraph("\u03C3", as_sub("E")),
      as_paragraph("range"),
      as_paragraph("\u0278")
    )
  )
```

```{r diagnostic-summary, results="asis"}
diag_sum <- readr::read_csv(here::here("tables/diagnostic_casestudy_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

flextable(diag_sum) %>%
  set_caption(
    "Summary of diagnostic procedures for the 6 case studies. Row 1 reports whether the calibration factor was significant from zero with \"S\", or \"NS\" otherwise. Row 2 reports the frequency that the true negative test passed. Rows 3 and 4 report whether there is a trend in calibration factors when estimated with new data (row 3) or fewer data (row 4). Trend is determined whether the slope of the linear regression of calibration factors was significantly different from zero (\"S\"), or not (\"NS\"). Text in parentheses of the first column indicates the desirable result. Asterisks indicate where the desirable result was not achieved."
  ) %>%
  width(j = 1, width = 2)
```

# Figures

(ref:fig-simple-example) Simple example illustrating the estimability of the indirect calibration factor in an index standardization model without comparative fishing. A predictive model for the population process is needed, a linear regression in this example, and is used to obtain the requisite degrees of freedom to estimate a vessel effect (at the dotted horizontal line) as a second intercept. This is a form of regression discontinuity design [@thislethwaite1960]. This figure is based on Figure 1 of @lee2010.

```{r simple-example, out.width = "3.5in", fig.cap="(ref:fig-simple-example)"}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("manuscript/figures/simple_example.png"))
```

(ref:fig-sim-grid) Simulated spatial density for a single year in the operating model, where the spatial correlation varies with the $\kappa$ parameter (decorrelation rate) of the Matérn covariance function. Grey circles indicate the location of 100 random sites for the simulated observations. The distance at which correlation of density decays is $\sqrt{8}/\kappa$ [@lindgren2011], with lower $\kappa$ value corresponding to larger spatial correlation range.


```{r sim-grid, fig.cap="(ref:fig-sim-grid)"}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("manuscript/figures/sampling.png"))
```

```{r rho2, fig.cap="Estimates of calibration factor, log(ρ), from the comparative fishing (CF, \"direct\") and the spatiotemporal model (ST, excluding CF sets, \"indirect\"). Horizontal lines indicate the 95% confidence intervals and dashed vertical lines denote zero."}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("manuscript/figures/rho_casestudy.png"))
```

```{r index-compare, fig.cap="Comparison of indices of abundance for six case studies based on vessel calibration method. The index is conditional on the catchability of the new vessel, operating in years after the vertical dashed line. Thus, index values after the vessel change are similar regardless of the calibration method. The indirectly calibrated index has larger confidence intervals because the standard error from the calibration factor is carried over to the error in the index through the delta method."}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("manuscript/figures/index_compare_ci.png"))
```

```{r rho-null, out.width = "4in", fig.cap="Estimates (points and 95% confidence interval linerange) of the indirect calibration factor (y-axis) when fitting the spatiotemporal model to data from only the new survey and estimating a dummy calibration factor. The estimation is repeated for various dummy years (x-axis) for each case study (panels). The calibration factor should not be significantly different from zero (dotted horizontal line) with the true negative test."}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("manuscript/figures/rho_null.png"))
```

```{r rho-ret, out.width = "4in", fig.cap="Estimates (points and 95% confidence interval linerange) of the indirect calibration factor (y-axis) when fitting the spatiotemporal model as more data from the new survey are available. The data set for the indirect calibration factor can increase as more survey data become available over time. In this retrospective analysis, the spatiotemporal model is fitted with all data from the old survey and from 1 to 6 years of the new survey (x-axis) for each case study (panels). Ideally, there is no trend in the indirect calibration factor over time. The horizontal dotted line is the direct calibration factor from comparative fishing and the shaded region is the corresponding 95% confidence interval."}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("manuscript/figures/rho_retrospective.png"))
```

```{r rho-gap, out.width = "4in", fig.cap="Estimates (points and 95% confidence interval linerange) of the indirect calibration factor (y-axis) when fitting the spatiotemporal model as the time gap between surveys increase (x-axis). The estimate may degrade as the time gap increases as the model must interpolate the population process across more time steps to estimate the calibration factor. The horizontal dotted line is the direct calibration factor from comparative fishing and the shaded region is the corresponding 95% confidence interval."}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("manuscript/figures/rho_gap.png"))
```

(ref:fig-sim-trend) Dot and line plots of the root mean square error (RMSE) in the index trends (y-axis) in the simulation study. The x-axis shows the error as new annual survey data is added to the spatiotemporal model (from 1 to 5 years). Circles with solid lines denote the RMSE from the indirectly calibrated index whereas crosses with dotted lines are from the uncalibrated index. Colours denote the spatial de-correlation parameter $\kappa$, where high values denote low spatial correlation. The circle shading (filled vs. open) denotes the dispersion parameter (lower values are more dispersed). Rows show three levels of catchability differences between vessels. Columns show the evolution of spatiotemporal field in the operating model.

```{r sim-trend, fig.cap="(ref:fig-sim-trend)"}
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("manuscript/figures/sim_trend_RMSE_retrospective.png"))
```
